utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. If you're ready, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, at one point, in fact several times, you say that the Muslim side did not have 122- and 150-millimetre artillery; is that so?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I said that we had not seen any of those within the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we call up 1D1542 in e-court. [No interpretation] We'll deal with it briefly. This is a report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command, dated 31 May. A cease-fire is in force, and in line 5, if we can scroll down, it says, I'll read it out: "At 10.15, from the direction of Mount Igman, the enemy fired a 155-millimetre shell at the sector of Krivoglavaca," et cetera, et cetera. Can we see the next page, please. Item 6: "Logistical support from the rear command post --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Have you found the English translation? Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is ...? You have a translation photocopied. Shall we put it on the ELMO? We have that noise again, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is starting again, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, let me tell you that the Defence and the Prosecution are engaged in talks to get a full list of all documents, and I believe this will shorten the waiting time in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate it very much. Very well. This is the, yes, translation. What page should we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can see the whole first page. Item 1, we see the cease-fire was violated. First of all, we need to see the top of the page. Display the whole page. [In English] Can you lift it a little bit? [Interpretation] Then it must be the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't hear a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, now are you hearing something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the paragraph that begins with: "At 1015 ..." Does it say about where the shell was fired from and the calibre? Is it 155?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Can you see this? Is it a report about shelling from a 155-calibre?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I can see it was a K-85 -- one K-155 shot from Igman, so that confirms what I said, and as far as we know, there was no 155 pieces of artillery within the city of Sarajevo because Igman is outside of Sarajevo, and I'm sure everyone knows this by now here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you where the fire from Mount Igman is directed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards areas that I cannot really ascertain. One should give me a map so that I can see where that actually fits in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the fire from Mount Igman is directed exclusively at the north, towards the Serb neighbourhoods of Sarajevo, does that sound plausible to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a doubt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, the artillery at Mount Igman is part of the Sarajevo theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was outside my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The shells were falling into your area of responsibility; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because my area of responsibility was the close proximity of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, we appeared to have agreed that from Mount Igman, the fire landed in Dobrinja, Ilidza, Rajlovac, and other Serb neighbourhoods of Sarajevo and nowhere else. Why else would this artillery have been there, except to shoot at the Serb neighbourhoods? Rajlovac, Ilidza, Vogosca and these neighbourhoods, were they part of your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, but I asked for a map to be showed to me to see where that is, Krivoglavci as well as Sarajevo. I would like to know what that means on the ground, because as far as I'm concerned, I don't know whether it is Lukavica, Ilidza, or other places that would have been held by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, we'll show that. Can we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher could kindly turn the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 6 and 7, can you raise the text a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see point 6: "There are shortages of food, especially foodstuffs for breakfast, and all calibres of ammunition"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are hearing some noise. My colleague says she's hearing some noise in French. The same should be true with the witness. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm listening to the French channel, and I also hear the feedback.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, can we prepare the translation of 1D1946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't think we can continue. It's better to have a break. I'm sorry again, Mr. Witness, but we need to take a break. We'll break for five minutes. I hope that everything could be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies yet again, Mr. Witness, for the inconveniences. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope you noticed on page 1 that it's the 31st of May, 1993. Would you please look at the consequences indicated in item 7, the consequences of this activity during cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The bottom of that page is casualties, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see there were also civilian casualties, two civilians dead and ten wounded, injured?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the French/Serbian translation is faster than the English translation, so both of you are somewhat overlapping. In any event, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D338, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 1D1946. There is a translation for that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting: Do you know that Hadzici is a neighbourhood of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is part of what is called Greater Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo has 10 municipalities. Hadzici is one of them. Do you know that the Serbs controlled Serb parts of Hadzici, which is a small part, whereas Pazaric is a Muslim area that the Serbs did not control?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Hadzici -- you're talking of several areas where there were Muslim areas and Serb areas within Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking: Do you know that Hadzici is a municipality of the city and that Hadzici contained an area called Pazarici, which was a Muslim neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, Hadzici was under the control of the Bosnian Muslims. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Muslims controlled the largest area. I just want to tell you that we have a document dated 12 March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not this document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not. It's 1D1946.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think, actually, the wrong document might be linked to that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Hadzici also in your area of responsibility, Hadzici as a city area, as a municipality, because your personnel visited that locality; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My area of responsibility went along the front-line as far -- or I should say that the front-line was surrounding the city as well as the airport.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should probably put this on the ELMO. Something's wrong with the number. The front-line also crossed Hadzici, between the Serbian part of Hadzici and Pazarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly look at this document, where it says they received 1.000 shells of 152 millimetres calibre? In fact, this is a confirmation of receipt. [In English] It is not on. [Interpretation] Can you see this, Witness? They're reporting that on the 10th of March, they received 1.000 grenades for a 152-millimetre Howitzer. So can we say, Witness, that the Muslim side was not sincere and frank when it told you what it had disposed of, what it had at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to reiterate that my main focus was on weapons of the government army, weapons that were within the confines of the city of Sarajevo. Earlier on, you said that the front-line in Hadzici was under my area of responsibility. I would like to remind you there was a special setup as far as the airport was concerned. And because the front-lines were rather tricky, it was difficult to follow them because you had a corridor leading towards the outside, towards Butmir, where the front-lines were no longer joined and they were actually discontinued. And in that area, my area of responsibility was the outer confines of the airport, but it seems that you haven't heard that when I first mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My understanding of it is that your area of responsibility was everything that was under the 1st Corps, the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps, and Sarajevo had 10 municipalities. And what about Ilijas, was that in your area as well; Vogosca, Ilijas, and so on, Pale?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, that's clear to me now. Now, let me remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't suppose you're going to admit this document, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you're well familiar with the Rules, Mr. Karadzic. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. Yesterday, we displayed 1D1943, where it says that they had a Howitzer battery, 122 millimetres, and a self-propelled Howitzer battery of 152 millimetres in the city, itself, so they didn't tell you about that. So I put it to you once again that they weren't sincere towards you, they weren't frank in what they told you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the quality of the information contained in this document, whether you laid face to it or not. I believe what I saw, what my men saw, and during the six months of my tour in Sarajevo, nobody noticed the presence of any heavy gun in the city of Sarajevo. I will maintain what I have said already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you see there that they have a battery -- a mortar battery, self-propelled Howitzer, 122-millimeter, and a Howitzer, 122 millimetres, a Howitzer battery, and that was in town? And I do believe that the Serb side told you all about all the weapons it had, whereas the Muslim side quite obviously tried to deceive you; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are the one who says and claim that this was in the city. I know it was the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps, but it extended outside the city. It had units somewhere else as well, not just inside the city. I don't know the numbers of the brigades, I don't know where they were located, apart from the 10th Mountain Brigade. I cannot tell you whether, indeed, based on this report by the head of the 1st Bosnian Corps, these batteries belonged to units or brigade stations within the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Shall we go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't state the name of any commander. It could have been a company commander, for that matter. I took care not to, and that's why I didn't ask for private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, anyway, do you see that we're dealing with the 3rd Motorised Brigade here? Now, the 3rd Motorised Brigade, was it in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you just a few moments ago that I could not remember, apart from the 10th Mountain Brigade, what the numbers were of the other brigades that were stationed within Sarajevo. I'm saying it again, and it may be the last time I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I was happy to learn yesterday that you knew everything about Sarajevo, but I see that you just remembered Caco, whereas the other moderates have been forgotten. But never mind, we'll establish where the area of the 3rd Motorised Brigade was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let me tender this into evidence first. Can it be admitted now, because it's directly related to what the witness was talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a basis to admit this. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've actually -- I've done some thinking and transcript reading about this document overnight, Your Honour, and on reading the transcript, Dr. Karadzic's intention became clearer. And now listening to this today, I actually think the document, as such, does meet the guide-lines that this Trial Chamber had articulated. The guide-lines say, at paragraph 11, that: "The general principle of admission does not rule out the possibility of admitting documents that challenge a witness's credibility, and the fact that the document goes to the witness's credibility may constitute sufficient nexus between the witness and the document for it to be admissible." And as I understand it today, as I understood it after reading the transcript, I think Dr. Karadzic is seeking to tender the documents as evidence that he alleges directly contradicts the testimony of the witness. And while I don't think it's direct evidence to the effect that the ABiH had weapons of the calibre that they've been discussing in Sarajevo, it looks like a valid attempt to impeach the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you do not oppose to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In short, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While this document was related to the credibility of the witness, the reason why the Chamber couldn't admit it was because we didn't have anything as regards the foundation of this document. But now that the Prosecution agrees with its admission, there seems to be a basis for the Chamber to admit it. As such, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. We have no objection, obviously, to the authenticity of the document either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. But I was informed that there's no full translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can make one available. We found one overnight as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. With that caveat, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't know where I went wrong and how I deserved such attention from the opposite side. I don't know if I will be able to repay it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, the previous document that was admitted was dated 31 May. We saw yesterday a couple of documents where the Sarajevo Romanija Corps informs the Main Staff that they are complying with a cease-fire, and now we are on the 1st of June, one of the documents covered in your statement. It's the Dobrinja football pitch attack. When was the first investigation into this case completed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I -- can we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What (redacted) about the type of shell, the type of projectiles?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the conclusion that was shown to you yesterday. In other words, on account of the, quote/unquote, "protection" or "obstacle" that was constituted by the buildings that were all around the football pitch, the conclusion was that the shell could only have been fired from a mortar. Given the crater and the fragments, (redacted) there were, indeed, mortar shell fragments, and because of the other technical data that were recalled yesterday, the only origin could be from the south/south-east of the football pitch, and the front-line was very close to the location of the incident because basically the front-line was on the other side of this building that was the obstacle. Obviously, it could only come from Bosnian-Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said something a little different yesterday, but right now I'm asking you about the calibre.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the calibre. I think we saw this in the document yesterday. Was it 82- or 120-millimetre? I can't remember. Maybe it was an 82-millimetre calibre. We'd have to see the document that we saw again -- that we saw yesterday again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that document, because we're going to ask for the whole document to be admitted. Can we now get 1D1543. You said yesterday that General Galic was an excellent officer and he wrote accurate reports on a daily basis about everything going on in his corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never stated that General Galic was an excellent officer, because I didn't at all agree with his orders. However, I said that he was a professional officer, because he was a professional serviceman and that he'd been trained to drafting accurate reports that he would send up to his hierarchy. But please remove the word of "excellent" that you fabricated and which I never uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you said "excellent military person," verbatim, although I can't give you the reference to the page. But I agree with you that he was an excellent military person. And due to a poor Defence he was sentenced to life, although he didn't even deserve to be charged. That's what you said spontaneously yesterday, anyway, and I'm just putting that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please refrain from making comment, Mr. Karadzic. What is your question, and do you like to stay in private session, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to stay in private session. Page 57 of yesterday's transcript, I'd just like the witness to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, I don't know if you've seen this page 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll read it for the witness. Shall we go back to open session? It's for you to ask. We'll go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is of transcript page 4.216, and it's from line 18. And there, Mr. Witness, you said: "I uncovered -- or I took during the 2009 hearings that General Galic was an excellent military person." And you give an account of what had happened every evening to his command. Well, I'm not sure whether it was a translation problem or not, but that's what is stated in the transcript. But that's not a big deal, and let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a problem with the translation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: CLSS will take a look into the matter. Move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to number 1. I don't know if we have a translation for this, but I'm going to read out only item 1. It says: "In the course of the day --" And this is dated 1 June: "In the course of the day, the enemy violated the cease-fire --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton is helping you a lot today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I apologise that I'm not a bit faster. It's just a matter of trying to locate the documents, and nothing more than that, but Mr. Reid is indispensable in that regard. I have a translation that could assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the date first. The date is the 1st of June. The time is 1700 hours. In paragraph 1, we see who did what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's wait until it functions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think I have the same document as the accused, because he's just said that this was drafted at 16 hours and I have the hour of 17 hours, so it's not the same document or else the accused is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think both documents said "1700 hours." Could the usher kindly take a look at the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17, yes, I said "17." The 1st of June, 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be that I misheard. Sorry, but I'm pretty sure I saw what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember that incident took place at 10.20 in the morning in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see it now. Paragraph 1 says: "In the course of the day, the enemy violated the cease-fire more than once, firing on our defence positions." And then there is a whole list of these violations, and not a single word mentions what happened in Dobrinja. Can we see the rest of the document? We can see that they opened sniper fire in Jezevo [phoen], Orahov Brijeg, the Vogosca factory sectors. We can move one page further, maybe even two pages. [In English] Okay, can we go on paragraph 7 and 8. [Interpretation] I would like to draw everyone's attention to all these elements. Let me not greet them all. Two fighting men got serious injuries to lighter injuries. Number 7 states the losses, and number 8 is the conclusion: "The corps forces respected the order on cease-fire in full. There was no response to enemy provocations. It is to be expected that intense sniper fire on civilian targets by the enemy will continue." Now, Witness, do you agree that in this document, which is strictly confidential, by 1700 hours there is not a single word about the incident that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, and I can understand that no mention or reference was made -- had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But not only that. It doesn't mention that fire was opened at all. In all other reports, we see when they opened fire, how much ammunition was expended, but here there's not a word about it. And this is a confidential report, and a corps commander should not omit anything when reporting to the Main Staff about developments in his area. Can we see that they never opened fire here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what is said in the report, but this may not reflect the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we have established, and I think we agreed, that the secret reports to the Main Staff were always exhaustive and accurate, and such an important thing like a case of armed attack in the neighbourhood would certainly have been mentioned there. Thank you. Can this document be admitted? It is relevant to the incident in question, and it's an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I find the document's authentic, Your Honour. And on that basis, I would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Likewise, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D340, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get 1D1933. We will now review all that anyone said about this event, to get a full picture. 1D19 -- yeah, that's it. I don't know if we have a translation. My learned friend Ms. Edgerton maybe knows. Let me read to you from the heading. It's the Foreign Ministry, the Secret Service, in other words, the National Security Service, the War Section of Ilidza. The date is the 1st of June, 1993, and they report -- if we don't have a translation, then let me read out a part: "On the 1st of June, 1993, we received new information from a completely reliability source about today's incident in Dobrinja. In the communication between two members of the so-called BH Army, one of which stayed in Dobrinja, we found out that one of the commanders of the so-called BH Army led out his units onto the parking-lot in the Vahide Maglajlic Street, in Dobrinja, 3, and that they organised the football match, in the course of which two shells had landed. According to the statement of the same person, out of the total number of the wounded, 50 members of the so-called BH Army were taken to the Kosevo Hospital, and nine dead are in the morgue in Dobrinja. The aforesaid person expressed the opinion that that commanding officer should be arrested and executed by firing squad." And then there is a nota bene from the National Security Service. At the bottom, and it says: "Through our source, we will continue to follow and look for new information regarding this incident." Is it the case that this football match was played by members of the BH Army, as this report says?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what is stated in this report by the Serbian Intelligence Service. That's all that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Dobrinja, there was a regular unit or regular units, and that's the place where the units leaving the city to go to Mount Igman assembled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we mentioned it earlier on. It was within my area -- well, actually, perhaps we should move to private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But certainly, Witness, you're not challenging, are you, the fact that the units of the 1st Corps went into the city and exited the city, and that sometimes they would appear at one theatre of war and sometimes in another area; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said. We did not notice that full units were leaving the town through the airport or were entering into the town. We just noticed that soldiers, on an individual basis, left the city or were trying to go inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll be presenting documents in due course where we can see orders to the effect that the units should return -- or, rather, leave Sarajevo and return to Sarajevo. We'll do that on another occasion, but let's now go back to the incident we were discussing. If you recall, and I think we looked at the document on our screens yesterday - I don't believe it's admitted - on the 22nd of May, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps ordered all officers and, if necessary, the police, to place all weapons larger than 12.7-millimetre calibres, so it was the document of the 22nd of May which meant there was no shooting after that date. Now, at 1020 hours, two shells fell. Let's look at the document again produced by the Prosecution yesterday. 11383 is the number, but there's a P number, a new P number, because it's an exhibit already. Can somebody help us out? 11383, but it was P1047 or 8, I believe. Three pages were admitted, but we should like to tender the entire document now, please. 11383 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was P1053.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you: On the 1st of June, you had an insight -- well, you investigated on-site, and then on the 2nd of June you issued a caution to the Serb side; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now let's see -- that's not the right document. Or, yes, let's see the entire document. Let's have the whole document displayed. 11383 is the number. This is just a part of it which was admitted and tendered by the Prosecution, but we need the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed that the whole document was numbered, in terms of 65 ter, it is 11383a, small A. Is that correct? I think we are looking at the first page, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if we're talking about the whole document. But if it is P053, then we just have three pages there. But the break is coming up now, so shall we leave it until after the break, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have before us the whole document of the investigation report. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, is this document familiar to you? Have you seen it before? Did you take a look at it during the proofing session with the Prosecution, for instance?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to draw your attention to the first two paragraphs: "On the 28th of June, 1993," and then the people mentioned, "were tasked to conduct an investigation into a mortar attack that happened in the Dobrinja district of Sarajevo on or about the 1st of June." So this is 27 days later; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And number 2, it says that they have received a copy of an analysis, and you mentioned this, and I'd like to draw your attention to F, paragraph 2(f), and I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Due to the fact that both rounds impacted into a macadam surface, the angle of descent and range cannot be determined." [Interpretation] So this is from the first investigation that was carried out by the UN representatives and handed over to this group doing the investigating; that is to say, that neither the angle of descent nor the range could be determined. Right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see at the bottom there that it says: [In English] "Attached to the crater analysis report, and that's showing the line of flight, suspected firing locations and points of impact for both rounds." [Interpretation] Now may we turn to the next page, please, and I'd like to remind you of what it says here, "suspected firing locations." Does it say "suspected"? Well, we're now on to the next page, but it said "suspected" there, didn't it, previously? Can we show the witness where it says "suspected firing locations." Do you see that, the sentence just before paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the sentence beginning with: "Attached to the crater analysis ..." Zoom out, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now turn to the next page, please. Lower down on that page, 4(c), let's look at that. Well, the whole document is interesting, but point C in particular: [In English] "There were a lot of people at the game, many of them young people who were participating and also spectators." [Interpretation] And towards the bottom there, there's mention here of Mr. Stekovic, and it says that it was exclusively residential in nature, the area, Dobrinja, and that they played on the stadium. Now may we have a look at page 447. We'll come back to Mr. Stekovic later, but 447 -- the last digits of the page I'd like us to look at next is 447. Next page. Thank you. And I'd like to draw your attention there to paragraph 9. I'm not going to read the names. It says: "At approximately 0907 hours on the 2nd of July, accompanied by," the gentleman whose name is stated there and the others: [In English] "We realised that all investigative materials related to this incident had been forwarded to the main police station in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] So the police station at Dobrinja: "... attended the police station where we met with this man, Kosevac [phoen], and they said that the material relating to this incident had been forwarded to the main police station in Sarajevo. May we turn to the next page now, please. Just a moment, please. Let's just look at paragraph 10 there. Let's stay with that page, paragraph 10, please: [In English] "While in attendance at the main police station ..." [No interpretation]: [In English] "... was informed by officials there that materials regarding the mortar attack were not presently available; however, they could be obtained at the Security Services Centre at 1400 hours, 2nd of July, 1993." [Interpretation] And then paragraph 11: [In English] "About 1405 hours of 2nd of July, 1993, accompanied by ..." And you see all that there, all the names: [In English] " ... to the Security Services Centre, where we met with," this guy whose name you see. "He advised us that there was no investigation conducted into the matter of civil authorities, and that the Bosnian military may have made inquiries into the matter. He added that his department was currently investigating the organisers of the tournament, and that he understood Bosnian TV may have video footage of the event. He commented that UNPROFOR authorities had attributed the incident to the Serbian military, and that that was sufficient for his department." [Interpretation] Do you agree that they did not conduct an investigation because it was sufficient -- the fact that the UN had ascribed this to the Serbs was sufficient, as far as they were concerned.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what is written on the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move on to the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So neither the local police station or the municipal or regional police station did anything. It was enough that the Serbs were accused, and they investigated who organised the football match, not who did the shooting. Is that what it says there in that previous paragraph; right? Well, the page isn't on our screens, but that's what it said. Now let's look at paragraph 14. I'm going to read part of it: [In English] "About 8.45 [sic] on the 4th of July, 1993, I received a copy of a map of Dobrinja from UNPROFOR officials, a copy which is attached as Annex 1. This map shows that the soccer game was held in a location surrounded on three sides by buildings (west, east and south). In addition, it was explained that there are Bosnian mortars located outside the hospital approximately 500 metres from the soccer location. However, these were not observed during our visit to Dobrinja area." [Interpretation] So did you know or notice that 500 metres away from the soccer location, they had their mortar position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an accurate memory of it, but it is quite possible. I underline that the mortar units, especially with the Bosnians, had this characteristic, that they would move them very often. They had no fixed position, which accounts for the fact that unlike the Serb artillery positions, we had not ascertained what the permanent locations were of the Bosnian mortar units because such did not exist. They would move them frequently so as to avoid being located and have a counter-battery fire fired on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 120 and 82 were probably on trucks. Now, the 60-millimetre -- a 60-millimetre infantry weapon, it can be carried on your back; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or then it was mounted on a vehicle. But a 60-millimetre can easily be taken on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's focus on paragraph 17: [In English] "At approximately 1014 hours on 5th of July, 1993, accompanied by Mr. Mocibob," and so on, "I attended Dobrinja. We were met with Mr. Dinko Bakal." [Interpretation] Now let's see what it says under C: [In English] "He heard the detonations and believed that they were caused by 82-millimetre mortars, but later discovered that they were, in fact, 60-millimetres mortar. "D. He assisted in evacuation of the wounded, most of whom were women, children, and civilian persons." [Interpretation] Now let's move on to the next page, and let's see what it says at the top there: [In English] "Although the site cannot be seen from the confrontation line, he believes that the person responsibility may have had the coordinates." And he says that: "There are no military targets nearby," and so on. [Interpretation] And now paragraph 19 down at the bottom there, 19 and 20, towards the end of the page: [In English] "Other investigative steps related to this case may include interviews with Serbian officials, as well as other witnesses." [Interpretation] And 20: [In English] "A further report will be submitted. Therefore, this report is pending." [Interpretation] Can we now agree that the report was not complete or final?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is up to the investigators. Indeed, if they say that they still had to interview Serbian officials, I don't know whether they did this or not, but apparently this is not part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now briefly go through, and I hope we can have yes-and-no answers, through what it says. We have a cease-fire enforced from at least the 22nd of May. That's one element. And we also have the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which is lacking in ammunition and is reporting that it is adhering to the cease-fire. And we have, on the 1st of June, at 10 -- 22 shells, grenades. Then we have proof of evidence that the Army of Republika Srpska, from its positions, could not see the area where the soccer game was being held, but that for such precise targeting you needed coordinates or they needed coordinates. And on the 1st of June, at 1700 hours, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is reporting, and in its report it makes no mention of any shooting. On the 2nd of June, then without a completed investigation, a warning is being issued, a letter to me from General Morillon, and a caution to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So this is being ascribed to the Serbs. And it was only on the 28th of June that UNPROFOR is giving a group of officers the task of investigating; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the investigation was requested by the highest echelon of the UN on location. I can't remember the name of the organ in charge of prosecuting or investigating into war crimes and the fact that this, as stated by this report, comes from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, we agreed that the best way -- or, rather, the best time to investigate an incident is straight after the incident took place, and here this is being done almost after four weeks, so almost a month was allowed to elapse. Now let's remind ourselves further. On the 2nd of July, this team went to the Dobrinja police station to take over the investigation material, and they were told that it was somewhere else. So they went to this other place, to the Sarajevo Police Station, to take over all the material in the Security Services Centre, and when they arrived there they were told an investigation had not been conducted because there was no need, since it was ascribed to the Serbs. Now, on the 4th of July, information receives UNPROFOR that 500 metres from the incident you had the BH Army mortars, and an analysis of the crater showed that there were two possibilities linked to 82- or 122-millimetre mines, whereas witnesses interviewed by UNPROFOR confirmed that they were 60-millimetre ones. So the only piece of information from the Serb side -- a document from the Serb side is that the MUP of Ilidza, the State Security, on the 1st of June, 1993, learned that two shells had fallen, and that the participants were soldiers, and that they were angry with the commander who organised the soccer game. And we see that the civilian authorities investigated the organisers of the soccer game and not the perpetrators of the crime, itself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what this document you submitted to me says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then further down, it advises that all the participants, that is to say, Stekovic and the others, were interviewed, that they were combatants. So all the names we have were the names of combatants. And now I'd like to tender this document into evidence in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the practice; we give the same number or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll add that, the remaining part to the already-existing parts, which will be Exhibit -- what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1053, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you accept that Mr. Izetbegovic, on the 21st of March of that same year, was in New York, attending a conference there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that we can now move back into open session. And perhaps already today or by tomorrow we will provide you with media reports which make it clear that we were all in New York at the time already as of the 17th or 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very important witness because he knows a lot of things, and he has admitted to that, to knowing the situation well. We're not going to lose any time by going into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you allow for the possibility that the Muslims from time to time bombed their own territory and their own people and their own units?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, on a few occasions we noticed that there were snipers firing within the city, and perhaps there were also mortar fire, namely, other weapons, that were rather suspect when we looked at them more closely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1953, please. We just need to take a short look at a document of the Muslim 1st Corps. This should not be broadcast. I would appreciate it. I don't know if we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This commander, the undersigned, is writing to UNPROFOR officers, and he says: "The resentment is caused by the claim that the BH Army, from its positions, is firing at the airport where UNPROFOR forces are based, and also at their own wretched people who are trying to leave the town and get to modest quantities of food," et cetera, et cetera. So this is a letter -- a response to the letter by the UNPROFOR, accusing them of shooting their own people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have the translation at least in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it again. It can be interpreted. Can we go into private session, and then we can read all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is a document -- a directive that I sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 11th of March, that is, a week before I left for New York to attend a conference. And I can draw your attention to paragraph 1. I order that a consignment and safe passage of a shipment be enabled to prohibit any misuse for military purposes of food supplies, crops, plumbing, and drinking water, reservoirs, as well as water dams; to abide by the Geneva Convention for the protection of victims of war, et cetera, et cetera, and to ensure that all army units familiarise themselves with the directive and comply. Do you agree that this is in conformity with the upcoming talks and the hope that we will achieve peace? Did you know or were you aware that I was issuing directives like this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the Serbian Army was not sending me their internal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you accept this is an authentic document issued 10 days before the incident that we are about to shed some light on now?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, if one looks at the date, 11th of March, it was about 10 days before the incident that you are going to talk about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this has already been admitted as Exhibit D104.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1976 is the next document I'd like to look at. 1D1976. This will be a document of the Muslim army, their Main Staff, the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How come we were not considered also to be a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Since you don't have the document, let me tell you. On the 16th of March, and we are drawing closer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could just have your indulgence for a couple of seconds, we can provide a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just as fast as technology works, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still amazing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask for the ELMO to be turned on again. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to draw the parties' attention to the entire document. It is extremely important for the events that would transpire in Sarajevo in the spring of 1993, but for the moment we are focusing on Sarajevo. It's a document from General Halilovic. Look at paragraph 1: "Order strictly confidential number 02/398-1, dated 15 March 1993, is null and void and was issued for propaganda purposes." And the preamble says: "Referencing the received order strictly confidential number ... dated 15 March 1993, regarding the cessation of hostilities, I hereby order:" And then it says that the order is null and void and was issued for propaganda purposes. All this would later result in the events around Cerska and Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this, this order by the commander of the Muslim army, and can you contrast it with the orders that I gave?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see -- I see "Mr. Halilovic," and I can see that he sent to the 2nd Corps. I believe that it was a corps that was based outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted? The cessation of hostilities was to apply in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he issues an order like this at the time when we are leaving to attend that conference in New York. He orders the cancelling of the cessation of hostilities and demands fierce offensive action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what question did you ask the witness about this document? All he said is that Mr. Halilovic sent this document to the 2nd Corps. That's all he said. What's the point of putting this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is why it's important: The United Nations mainly contributed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. Put your question to the witness instead of making a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, a short question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the cessation of hostilities and the cease-fire applied in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall precisely this very cease-fire. If one looks at the document that you have showed me and that you signed, there was probability a cease-fire that had been agreed upon at the highest level, but I do not recall exactly the date of the cease-fire. Over six months, I experienced so many cease-fires that I don't remember them all by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Izetbegovic set the condition? He will go to the conference if a cease-fire is achieved? Do you remember that? It was made public.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this because I believe that these were negotiations that were dealing with the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I understand correctly, if I look back to the text that you showed us, and these negotiations went far beyond my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. But I want to ask if you knew about this duplicity, this double-play, that they accept a cease-fire and a cessation of hostilities, and then the next day send out secret documents telling people to disregard it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Bosnia, I soon realised that all the parties that were there were playing double-play. So this double-play from the Muslims does not surprise me, but I also experienced some from the other parties as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember confirming that five days after this document, after this order, there was an attack by the 10th Mountain Brigade against Serb positions and Serb communications, or roads, as you understood it? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, we talked about this at length already. Unfortunately, the document that you're putting forward is addressed to the 2nd Corps, and the 10th Mountain Brigade did not belong to the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This violation of the cease-fire applies to the entire territory, obviously, because it was a unit of the 1st Corps that violated the cease-fire on the 21st and also earlier, as you will see later.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well be. The one of the 21st was blatant, if there was a cease-fire then. Since you are saying that, I believe that there was a cease-fire that was underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the 10th Mountain Brigade attacked Serb positions; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still think it's too much of a stretch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As to the so-called double-play on both sides, the witness confirmed to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Peripheral relevance, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you're satisfied with the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So on that basis, the Chamber will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now get 1D1511. 1D1511.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, let me inform you that it was a report to the Main Staff, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, dated 19 March, just briefly for you to see the activities of the enemy side, the Muslim side, on the 19th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Translation is coming up, Your Honour. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very, very much. I hope we, too, will soon get the translations that are available.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These are all CLSS translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this. It's the 19th of March to the Main Staff. Paragraph 1: "Over the past period, the enemy launched strong artillery attacks on the Ilidza sector with 15 mortar shells, the Azici sector with 30 mortar shells, Grbavica with 12 mortar shells, the Ilijas sector with 60 mortar shells, and Lukavica, 7 mortar shells. "The enemy mounted strong combined infantry and artillery attack on the positions of the Rajlovac Light Infantry Brigade in the Sokolje sector." And if we can see lower down the page -- no, no, paragraph 4: "This is how Serbs are getting killed during cease-fire. Losses: One dead, ten wounded, all from the Rajlovac Brigade; three dead and six wounded civilians from Ilijas." Witness, sir, did you ever hear from Serbs that those cease-fires were very expensive to us, they cost us dearly because we died in greater numbers during cease-fires than during combat?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we move to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) Do you agree that the Army of Republika Srpska responded only after such losses, and they did not respond to threats before they suffered losses; they observed the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you retaliated, it means that you were under attack. So you could only retaliate when you were under attack. And, indeed, I do not recall of any specific violation of the cease-fire. Through those reports, one can see that there were perhaps no violations on the cease-fire. Why not? But I do not recall everything. By the same token, you remind me that there was a violation of the cease-fire by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, and can I then call up another one? I think we can move into open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. While we are going back to open session: Ms. Edgerton, can I see this document, the first page? What is your observation, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, on the authenticity of the document, I have no objection. As to the relevance, I think it's marginal and had little relation to the ultimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, because this is two days before the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds it relevant, and then we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1929, please. We will skip a little and move to the 6th of April, and then we'll go back to the 20th and 21st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 6 April, this is a letter sent by General Milovanovic, chief of staff of the VRS, to the UNPROFOR in Zagreb and to Kiseljak. Do we have it? This is it. We can look at the whole document, but the text in the box is important. I can read it in English or you can read it for yourselves: [In English] "On the 6th of April, 1993, while we were trying to talk about the establishment of peace, the cease-fire was again violated by Muslim-Croatian forces." [No interpretation]: [In English] "The outcome of today is eight dead, eight lightly and two heavily wounded soldiers. "Snipers were very active, especially in the city of Sarajevo." [No interpretation]: [In English] "Do you think that it can be endured much longer?" [Interpretation] Therefore, the Army of Republika Srpska has instructions to hold out as long as they can, and General Milovanovic is actually reproaching me for asking them to withhold fire, but they can't stand it much longer because they have great losses, eight dead and eight wounded -- ten wounded. Do you agree that this is intolerable?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were in the midst of a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the first sentence talks about the restoration of peace, and it says the cease-fire was again violated, which means that a cease-fire had been in effect.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if there was a cease-fire, it was the responsibility of those who had agreed upon the cease-fire to break it, depending on the situation, but it was up to them. It was their responsibility, and it was according to their assessment that they should decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see these localities in the second paragraph, Sarajevo, Rajlovac, Nedzarici, Dobrinja, Lukavica? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we move to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 1D1977, please. And we've come to the 20th of March now, 1993, and the document is from the Muslim army. Yes, that's it, 2774. We don't seem to have the translation of it; is that right? Then I'd like to tell you what the document is about, and we'll have it translated: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina armed forces, 1st Corps, Sarajevo Communications Centre." And then it says "the Command of the Operative Group Igman." What's that? Yes, Igman, the 20th of March, 1993. Regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can stop there, Witness, and ask you this: You said that the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was derived from the JNA, the model of the JNA, and that's how it functioned. Do you agree that the structure of the Muslim Army of BiH was also modelled on the JNA example and that the officer cadre was from the Yugoslav People's Army and the army was made up of the former reservists of the JNA? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted, first of all, that there were very few professional career officers. And by the way, yesterday you expanded on the case of the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade, who was far from being a professional officer, which you and I both know, so I think they took on a lot -- a certain number of people who knew how to fight, and apart from them, they would resort to some kind of mobilisation of men to turn them into soldiers after a short training. But they were not only reservists; they were also people with no prior military experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this regular combat report of the 1st Corps, does it remind you of regular combat reports of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? It's the same structure. First of all, you have information about the enemy under number 1 and then under 2, and so on; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Well, I can't -- I do not read Serbo-Croat, so I don't know whether this is intelligence on the enemy. But if you say so, I'll gladly believe you. But I believe that, nevertheless, there was, within the government's army, a number of officers with some military experience and who were able to take on all the formal aspects of a professional army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And under 1, "Information about the enemy," I'll just read out the first sentence: "Today, the Chetnik activities --" They refer to the Serbs with the term "Chetnik," although the Chetniks were the Royalist Army during World War II and we abolished both the Chetniks and Partisans, but they referred to us as Chetniks: "Now today Chetnik activities were of a lesser intensity compared to the previous day." And then it goes on to say where the shooting took place, but what is important is under number 2, information about our own forces: "Pursuant to an order from the commander of the Operative Group Igman, our artillerymen opened fire from a 130-millimetre cannon with two projectiles, 105-millimetre Howitzers with four projectiles, and a cannon Howitzer, 152 millimetres, with 25 shells, against targets asked for by the commander of the 1st Corps. The Chetniks returned fire in the area of infantry weapons with four projectiles, MB-82. We shot at Chetnik positions in the area of Orlovac, where the Chetniks were setting up new firing positions. Our artillerymen used 82- and 120-millimetre mortars, firing five shells at the village of Vojkovici and the Sumanska [phoen] School. With rapid intervention from our fighters, we were able to localise a fire that broke out in Lasica," et cetera, "Sabro Haskovic, who was the Chief of Staff of the operative group."

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed, this report comes from 1st Corps units, which confirms (redacted) that the 1st Corps had units also outside of Sarajevo, because this one is Mount Igman, and actually I didn't know that there was a Sumanska School in Zenica [as interpreted], but if you say so, I gladly believe you. And probably they fired on this school in Ilidza. And I see that in spite of the cease-fire that had been violated by the Bosnian forces, the Serbian forces fired back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see that they returned fire at their artillery pieces using four projectiles and their firing positions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be that their fire was more accurate than the Bosnian fire. That's what I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree that Vojkovici was also -- well, that it was between Butmir and Hrasnica, that that's where the location was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this document into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification, unless it is objected to? Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D346, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we go into open session, let me ask you this: Would you assess this as being intensive activity, with shells falling on Serb positions? And this is from their sources, so there can be no doubt; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What subject would you like to speak about regarding my estimate of this activity, on Bosnian or Croat or Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to put before you a claim. I'm going to put something to you. You might know about it; you might not. This is what I state: that Mr. Izetbegovic was against any negotiations, that the incidents took place either just before some conference or during the conference, itself, and that served his purpose to interrupt the conference. Do you have any ideas about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed this, I observed, and I said so in previous reports, that indeed during negotiations there was often disproportionate use of artillery on either side, no matter who had started the artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I tell you that the Serbs wanted to have agreements signed as soon as possible because they had no further ambitions of taking control of any more territory, would that sound logical to you, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to assess political statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then we'll leave the political arena and move on. Now, this is already the 21st of March. 1800 hours is the time. We don't seem to have a translation, unless Ms. Edgerton surprises me pleasantly again. Not this time; very well. So I'll read it out. This is from the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, strictly confidential, then the number and date, which is the 21st of March, 1993. Regular combat report as of 1800 hours, the situation up to 1800 hours. And the first sentence, it says: "From the direction of Mojmilo, an 82-millimetre mortar was fired and multiple rocket-launcher, targeting the Slobodan Princip Seljo Barracks. At around 1700 hours, five shells, 82-millimetres, fell in the area of Pavlovac [phoen], eight fighters wounded," and so on. May we now move on to paragraph 2. It says: "The unit which carried out the attack was open to crossfire from Igman, Dobrinja, and Mojmilo." And now paragraph 6 next, please: "The rear security," and then it says, "units of the corps need replenishment with ammunition, fuel, and reserve parts, spare parts." Can you see, Witness, that there's not a single word -- no mention at all of shelling in the center of Sarajevo, that General Galic makes no mention of that at all? Or, rather, this is his deputy. Colonel Marcetic is the name.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could answer your question if I had a translation into English of the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we turn to the next page of this document. I read it out, and the interpreters certainly translated it accurately. But let's move on to the next page. This is in addition to the regular combat report, that is to say, after 1800 hours. Colonel Marcetic received more information about another brigade. May we move down the page, please. That's right. And it says: "During the afternoon --" Point 1: "During the afternoon, the positions of the artillery of the Kosevo Brigade, Nahaversko [phoen] Brdo, was shelled by 14 mortar grenades and four projectiles fired from a ZIS cannon from the direction of Kum -- Hum, Zuc, and Orlic. Inflammatory grenades set fire to a forest around the firing positions of the artillery. The Kosevo Brigade is therefore relocating its artillery pieces and establishing line communications. Fierce artillery attack was carried out along Elevation 703 at Brijeg, with -- a Browning and other weapons were used to shoot from the direction of Hum, Sip, and Kobilja Glava."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not a word there about the shelling of the old city, Witness. And let me remind you that we were in New York, attending the conference. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only believe the reports from the UNMOs who were then present, spread over a number of observation posts in -- around Sarajevo and in the Greater Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Witness, according to these reports, there was heavy fighting, and there is no mention of that in any of the reports. And you'll see a report from the 1st Corps next. The Muslim report makes no mention of that either. So do you exclude the possibility of -- well, the translation wasn't correct.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question? I didn't understand it very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He hasn't finished his question. But could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So according to what is said here about the incident of the 21st of March, it was heavy fighting with 2.000-odd shells, no mention of that is made either in the media - we have agency reports - it's not mentioned by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and now you'll see that not even the 1st Corps mentions any of that. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, a redaction of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me return to the reliability or credibility of the system of observers that had been set up around and within Sarajevo. As all UN forces, there were people hailing from various countries. They were professional servicemen. They had been trained to observe artillery fire, incoming fire or outgoing fire, so I totally rule out any error from them that would concern several thousands of shells. They may have made mistakes as to a score, or even 200 or 300 shells, okay, but they could not have reported on 2.400 shells -- they can't have been wrong throughout and that only 200 or 300 shells had been fired on that day. So I really fully believe -- I give credence to all the UNMO reports, the other reports being, of course, sort of biased reports because they had been drafted by the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask how we are with time? This is a very precious opportunity for the Trial Chamber to get a full picture of the events in Sarajevo, and we still haven't touched upon many things from the cross-examination, from numerous witness statements, and the work on the maps. We would need to present a series of maps here so that the Trial Chamber can finally understand what Sarajevo really is and see what was located where. Can we get more time, perhaps, and finish this nicely tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I entered the courtroom just now, I was advised that you have had three hours and twenty minutes so far. So you have still one hour and forty minutes, and we'll see how -- where we'll be at the end of the five hours and see. But how many more hours do you anticipate in order to finish your cross-examination at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hoping to finish tomorrow, leaving perhaps some time for redirect by Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll see how you get on with the evidence by the end of today, and we'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be admitted, the 21st of March report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and an appendix to it? This is the supplement. We can also see the first page again for you to refresh your memory. Let's see the first page. Thank you. This is a report of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the Main Staff on the 21st of March, status at 1800 hours, and the supplement speaks about the events in the Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the witness wanted to see a map in relation to this report, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no objection to this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it -- admit it and be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit MFI D347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D1981, 1D1981. This is a report from the same day, a report by the 1st Corps of the BH Army. If the Prosecution does not have a translation, then I will read aloud the passages that I believe to be important.
