utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll put it on the ELMO. Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the whole document? Oh, it's on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's dated 21 March 1993, and in the first paragraph the corps notifies the command of the corps about the fire exchanges on that day, and it says the Chetniks, in fact, the enemy, launched a fierce artillery attack early in the morning on the 4th Motorised Brigade's area of responsibility, and this brigade was outside of Sarajevo. The enemy fired tanks, carriers and Praga self-propelled anti-aircraft guns from the direction of Gavrica Brdo, Kula, and so on, and sports airfield. There's a mistake here in this translation. It was actually against the defence area of the 4th Motorised Brigade, not the area of responsibility. An area of responsibility is wider than a defence area. They claim two shells containing chemical poison landed. That's not true. But we see also what kind of movements were executed, et cetera. Can we now see Article 2. So in the original, it says "defence area." That means on the lines. And then in the middle, it says: "On request -- at the request of the 1st Corps Command and for the purpose of supporting our forces in the general areas of Nedzarici, Stup, Azici, our artillery fired on targets as follows: "1. A 152-millimetre Howitzer fired 60 shells on the targets of TAT, Otes, a railway bridge at Zeljeznica. "2. Following authorisation from the 1st Corps Command, a multiple rocket-launcher, with 107-millimetre calibre, fired seven missiles on the Golo Brdo area. "The Chetniks responded by firing five 105-millimetre Howitzer shells on Malo Polje, with little effect." And then it goes on to say: "In combat so far, we've had 21 injured fighters and four dead." I've finished this quote. Do you see that all this is happening outside the urban area, outside the populated area; it's fire on lines?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I understood, and if I can recollect vividly what happened, this has to do with the western part of the Greater Sarajevo area. It's the western side of the airport and, more specifically, west or north-west, in the airport area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're right about that. It's all very close, and the shells were obviously coming from Mount Igman and they were falling, obviously, in the urban part. And the response was against their defence lines, not their areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the difference between "lines" and "defence lines"? I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Defence lines" and "defence areas" are one and the same things, but it's not the same thing as "area of responsibility." "Area of responsibility" is what we have in the English translation here mistakenly, and it's a much wider area than defence area. Defence areas and defence lines are considered to be the same in our terminology.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you will, all countries do not use the same words, but I think I understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that an area of responsibility is a broader concept than an area of defence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my country, we do not talk about defence areas. We talk about front-lines. Perhaps that's what you're talking about. The front-line is the line where you are in contact with the opponent, and the area of responsibility, indeed, goes deeper in the friendly setup.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From all these documents, both Serbian and Muslim, is it evident that fire is directed against legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, in the western part of the city this is what had been observed by the UN Military Observers, and this corresponded to combat actions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D348, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now call up 1D1514. While we're waiting: This will be a report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, a regular combat report at 1400 hours, addressed to the Main Staff, covering the 21st of March. That is the day after the incident. If the Prosecution does not have a translation, shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I heard the printing is going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's right, and we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see that this is the 21st of March, 1993, a report to the Main Staff at 1400 hours? The first paragraph says: "In the course of the day, the enemy continued intensive fire from artillery against Ilidza, which was targeted by about 200 projectiles, causing losses among civilians, both dead and wounded." Point 2 -- sorry, point 3: "The status on the territory without major changes. The safety of citizens is in jeopardy due to intensive fire from enemy artillery against populated areas." But there is nothing in this report firing on the city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, indeed. If I translate into military terms paragraph number 2, indeed, the Romanija Corps must have launched an offence operation because it reached lines, and it also says that the Ilidza Brigade is engaged on an offensive operation against Stup or in the direction of Stup. So there you go. But you know as well as I do that in this area, there were a lot of urban dwellings, and, as usual, there must have been a lot of collateral damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we've heard here from witnesses, beginning with April 1992 and onwards, that attacks at Ilidza are staged from Otes, and finally the VRS took this Otes and removed this threat. There were constant attacks before that, and we have plenty of documentation about that. But what I want to underline here is that 200 projectiles fell on Ilidza. Did this point find its way into the observers' reports?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that as myself, you saw the document that we saw yesterday, which was very clear, very precise. And there was the assessment of the sector commander which was also very clear, as we could see it in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid the observers did not really remark upon projectiles falling on Serbian neighbourhoods. But this is a report from the day after. Two hundred shells fell on this neighbourhood, Ilidza, and I'm sure you would have noticed and reported if those had been Serbian shells.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I think we're going astray. I don't quite understand the point of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, my main thrust is to see what, in Serbian and Muslim regular combat reports for the 21st of March and around that date, what is contained about fire against civilian targets. There's nothing of the sort, is there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time, and I'm trying to read it and to interpret it. I see that this is a report on a situation that happened at 1400 hours on the 22nd and not on the 21st. And as far as I'm concerned, I believe that if the Serbian force procedure was the same, we are only dealing with what happened on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the point is there's no trace, either in Serbian or Muslim regular combat reports, about an event of this magnitude. Now, Witness, is it the case that in order to put an end to a peace conference they didn't like, is it possible that Muslims staged an attack on their own people and their own installations, as they have done more than once?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not want to speculate on manoeuvre plans of the Bosnian side. What is certain is that the target of their initial attacks, namely, in the area of the 10th Mountain Brigade, when they were firing at the supply route to Pale, they could be assured that there would be a strong response from the Serbian forces, because all military men that were in the area knew full well that the Serbian forces were very good at sustaining --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or at applying, correction of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- artillery fire, but they didn't have sufficient infantry to respond through that means. And we actually realised on several occasions that when the BH Army was launching offensive attacks, the Serbs would mainly respond by launching artillery fire and by pounding, through the artillery, in order to make sure that the BH Army attack would stop. This is my comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not related to 21st of March, and the witness did not comment on anything about the document. So I find the Chamber is not satisfied with its relevance. As such, we'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we get 1D1860. Oh, sorry, it's D336. It's already an exhibit, a document by Colonel Wilson. I think he later became brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, let me ask you, Witness: Do you recall that the incident in the bread line served to put an end to the Lisbon Conference in May 1992, the 27th May 1992? Do you remember that while we were negotiating in Lisbon, there was an incident in the bread line, and it served as a reason for terminating the conference?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1992. I'm not asking you about your direct knowledge. I just want to see if you remember, because I want to point out some analogies.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember that. I was not there in person. I cannot recall, and I'm not in a position to talk about it, given that I have no information whatsoever regarding this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will show you very soon a document that indicates that you were normally informed about incidents from 1992, and you referred to them later, but, of course, one can't remember everything. Can we see lower in this document? The BH Army overview of military situation. This is the military situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and forecasts. In the middle, it says: "The BH Army offensive in Sarajevo would appear to remain on hold." Can we now get the next page? Did you notice this was the 21st of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at paragraph 6: [In English] "No major developments --" [Interpretation] I won't read it aloud. Everyone can read it. These are forecasts of Serbian objectives and intentions, and it is estimated and forecast that the Bosnian Serb army would remain in a defensive posture and rely on its superiority and indirect fire, as you confirmed a moment ago yourself, to deflect any BH Army offensive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it fits in with what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see lower down about the BH Army? This passage was about the Army of Republika Srpska. Now we see the BH Army at paragraph 9: "BiH Army forces will ..." [In English] "BiH Army forces will, as a priority, continue to apply pressure to disrupt BSA lines of communication and strengthen their links to the Srebrenica and Gorazde pockets in Eastern Bosnia ..." [Interpretation] Further down, it says: [In English] "They would also assist in ensuring BSA compliance with territorial agreement and place BiH Army forces in an advantageous position for a resumption of hostilities which they probably regard as inevitable." [Interpretation] So this was a week before the commencement of a major combat there began on the 31st of January, and this forecast by Colonel Wilson, later General Wilson, was pretty much on the ball?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that, in hindsight, it was pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see from these last few sentences that I read out that the Muslim army believed that once territorial agreements are reached, they will be in a good position to continue hostilities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please. The second paragraph of paragraph 11: "BH Army forces ..." [In English] "BH Army forces may be prepared to launch an offensive using their troops without Croat support. If they believe their position in peace negotiations is so weak, they must provoke for an intervention." [No interpretation]: "In summary, BH Army forces military objectives are assessed as:" [No interpretation]: "D. Launch an offensive in the Sarajevo area if they consider their bargaining position in negotiations untenable and intervention is the only resource [sic]." [No interpretation]: [In English] "Continue to re-arm and build up forces and resources for a resumption of war when they are in a more advantageous position."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I won't bother you any more with this document, but it's obvious that UN analysts estimated quite correctly that the BH Army will be pushing offensives, and even if a territorial agreement is reached, then the Serbs withdraw to the provinces assigned to them, they would continue the war, whereas the Serbian side would opt for defence. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I would like to thank you for talking abut how good the UN members were at forecasting events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document has been admitted. Could we now call up 1D1470. This comes after the forecast we looked at earlier. It's a regular combat report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, dated 31 January 1993. I don't know if we have a translation. Courtesy of Ms. Edgerton, we will get a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have quite a system. Thank you very much, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to recall that the OTP and the Defence team are negotiating an exchange of documents that have already been translated, so as to facilitate everyone's work. Let's see what the translation is like. It says that: "In the afternoon, the enemy carried outer a powerful artillery operation against the Ilidza area with about 40 mortar shells firing from Kovaci and Glavogodine, against the Rajlovac area with 16, 82-millimetre mortar shells from the Zuc area," et cetera. And then point 2: "In a successful counter-attack, units of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade managed to push back the enemy's line of defence in front of the village of Mrkovici, between 500 and 800 metres." You can read the rest of it. However, in paragraph 3.1, it says a UN member, who I won't mention, protested because the UNMO building at Brijesce Brdo, which clearly bore the UN flag, had recently been subjected to artillery fire: "He was told that the SRK Command did not have the locations of their observation posts and asked that they be to submit to them, which would enable us to secure them from our artillery. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I may be mistaken, but I think we're in open session. Aren't we, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there's nothing there that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They did not know where the location of the observation posts were, as it's stated in this document, but all those observation posts had a large UN flag, so I believe it was not very difficult even if you did not have the exact coordinates of the observation posts, and I would doubt about that. But it was quite easy to know where they were and to shelter them. So as far as I'm concerned, I should like to say that every time observation posts were subjected to artillery fire, I would believe that these were voluntary fire. And they knew full well what they were doing, those who were firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see this document, which is a secret report to the Main Staff, says the reverse, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But look at point 6. They insisted that an inspection be allowed of a communications, and they were told that there were sabotage terrorist groups there, which is correct, because I didn't use the road anymore. And then point 7, they particularly insisted that the container be removed because it was obstructing traffic, and their response was to say that the container was set up as a protection from sniper fire. And in both documents, it says that it will be removed -- or this document says that in point 7: [In English] "They were told that we were not aware of the agreement with General Gvero. If it is correct, we will remove the container to the side of the road or place three metal plates parallel to the road in order to protect ourselves from the snipers."

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment on this? Firstly, I'm rather surprised, to say the least, as I said this before -- the Serbian forces were part of a professional army, and I would be surprised that they would not know where the UNMOs were positioned in their OPs, so that is really quite a doubt in my mind. And, secondly, I recalled to you that if we were so concerned about the container in the Kasindolska Street, it was because it was the very spot where the Bosnian vice-prime minister had been assassinated by a soldier [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that regardless of a number of professional officers, it wasn't an office -- well, there weren't enough professional officers in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; would you agree with that? There were officers, but were there a sufficient numbers of professional officers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: By a Serbian soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the officers (redacted) in the Romanija Corps were former JNA officers, and I believe that the JNA was a professional army. And there seemed to be quite a few of them. It may be that there were less of them in the combat units. I couldn't ascertain that because I could not access the Serbian combat lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we agreed, did we not, that the Muslim officers came from the JNA as well; right? Where was Delic from, Halilovic, Hadzihasanovic, Hajrulahovic; were they high-ranking officers of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not senior JNA officers. All the generals in the Bosnian Serb Army were JNA soldiers. The generals from the Bosnian Army that (redacted) were former majors or captains of the Serbian Army, but I'm sure that this is not the topic or one of the issues of this trial and that we may be going astray. I could talk about this at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But -- is this document an exhibit already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so. We'll admit it, unless it is objected to. He talked about the visits. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D349, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 1D1940 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Witness, let me ask you this: Do you agree with what other witnesses have stated here, and I think you said it at one place, that the combat composition of Sarajevo Romanija Corps were ordinary people doing their job, and that they would go up to the lines in shifts when their turn came; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think you totally misunderstood me. I was speaking about the Bosnian 1st Corps. As to the Romanija Corps from Lukavica, what I could see, and especially so when I went to artillery battery positions without you knowing it being said by the side, I saw that there were reservists or people doing their military service, but I do not think that they could go back home because a number of them hailed from Sarajevo proper.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on the 31st of January, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps asked to be sent the coordinates of observation posts, and they were sent. And with this document, the Sarajevo Romanija -- the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the next day, that is to say, the 1st of February, is sending all brigades of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment, and everybody else, this and says: [In English] "We requested and received the exact coordinates of UNPROFOR's observation posts, both on our side and the Turk side." [Interpretation] They're referring to the Muslims as Turks here. So there we have all the observation posts, and it says at the bottom: "After you receive these coordinates, inscribe them on the maps." [In English] "Familiarise your immediate subordinates, especially commander of the Artillery Battalion, with their exact location, and prevent firing against the observation posts, especially prevent artillery fire against them, under any condition, in any way and by anyone's side. "After UN Military Observers' request from any observation post in our zone, i.e., on our side, offer maximum protection and assistance to UN members. "Sites of observation posts coordinates are strictly confidential by its character, and it must not fall in possession of unauthorised persons." [Interpretation] Do you see that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps reacted promptly, straight away? The next day, it sent out the coordinates and asked that they be introduced onto the maps, and gave strict orders not to open fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only congratulate the Romanija Corps for such an attitude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, since it is related to the document which we already admitted, i.e., the Exhibit D349, the Chamber is of the view that this can be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, only on the basis of that link, there's a -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D350, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 65 ter 12359, please. 65 ter 12359. And while we're waiting, let me inform you that it is a regular combat report of the 3rd of February, 1993. That means from the 31st of January -- on the 31st of January, we had that meeting with the colonel, and on the 1st of February the coordinates were inscribed. On the 3rd of February -- the 3rd of February is this document, and I'd like us to turn to page 3, please. And may we go briefly into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 1D1491, please. While we're waiting, and that's a document dating back to that same period, but let me ask you this in the meantime:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Muslim forces used the Marsal Tito Barracks for their firing positions and for opening fire at the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier on the protests from General Sidorenko in 1992 to General Siber and the demand that they be removed from the radars and Marsal Tito Barracks. And this is a regular combat report, dated the 4th of March, to the Main Staff, sent by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Perhaps there's a translation. Does the Prosecution have it? I really do envy the Prosecution. They have everything, and we have nothing. [In English] If you can put it a little bit down to see the head. Okay, then you lift it a little bit. Okay, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see what it says there: "During the day, the enemy did not respect the cease-fire and fired from the Srhinje and Visocica sector at civilian targets in Ilijas and Podlugovi, firing 15 shells. Similarly, an enemy 120-millimetre mortar fired from the Marsal Tito Barracks at civilian targets in Grbavica. There was an infantry attack," et cetera, et cetera. So we are claiming that the Marsal Tito Barracks was regularly used as a place from where to fire at our positions from, and you can see that our civilian targets were also shot at. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two things to tell you. First thing: As I said earlier on, the Bosnians were endeavouring to protect their mortars by making them as mobile as possible. Well, whether they fired them from the vicinity of the Marsal Tito Barracks, that's no surprise at all to me, but that was not a position, a mortar position, all the more so because that's where the Ukrainian Battalion was stationed, and I don't think that they were particularly favourable to the Bosnians. Second thing: You remind me of the Marsal Tito Barracks, and maybe we could speak about the fact that there were radars, artillery radars, in the barracks, aimed at detecting artillery fire. As soon as they were set up by the Ukrainian Battalion, they were silenced and damaged by artillery fire that, no doubt, did not come from the Bosnian side. But maybe I'm teaching you something here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that we have friendly feelings towards Ukraine, and we can also say that the Serb side would not have any motive to do them any harm. But while we're on the subject, let me ask you this: We had witnesses here who said that there did exist certain differences in how the individual nationalities viewed events in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document. The witness has just confirmed that there was the possibility of them not having permanent but temporary firing positions, and that they moved around and hid behind the barracks. And that's our experience too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness didn't confirm anything about the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he couldn't have known about this document because it was strictly confidential. But as a phenomenon as what was going on, that's something that he confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not admit this document. I note the time, Mr. Karadzic. You have spent about four hours twenty minutes so far, a bit more than that, but how much longer would you need tomorrow to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two to two and a half sessions. If not two and a half, then at least two sessions. And I promise that it will be of interest to the Trial Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It may depend on the remainder of the cross-examination. But how much -- how long would you expect your redirect examination to be, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Twenty minutes at the outside, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's try to conclude the witness's evidence by the end of second session tomorrow. So you will have about two hours, in the region of two hours. So we'll continue, Mr. Witness, tomorrow afternoon. And there's one final administrative matter to discuss, albeit in the presence of the witness. Yesterday, when I informed the parties as to the sitting schedule, I was mistaken; that on the 15th of July, there's no courtroom available to sit from the morning. So the 15th July, we'll rather sit in the morning -- in the afternoon shift, i.e., from 2.15 to 7.00 p.m. But on 8th, 16th, 19th, 20th, and 21st and 22nd of July, there seems to be a possibility for the Chamber to sit 9.00 to 3.00, so we'll sit -- do so in that way whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I may be allowed to say that I prefer the afternoon sessions. But I leave that to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us why it is so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be my biorhythm, as such. I work better in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, we'll consider the matter tomorrow afternoon. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a matter that didn't need to be dealt with now, but I didn't want to let more time go by before referring to the e-mail I sent on the 17th with respect to the Assembly sessions referenced in Dr. Donia's reports. So I just didn't -- thought that we shouldn't let that slip off the radar screen for so long since there was an indication that we had intended to address it in the following week. Not something we need to deal with now, but just a reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
